utterances.text: Good evening, Honorable Mayor Kate and Members of City Council. John Stefanski Assistant City Manager I'm here tonight with Mel Burnett, our housing and homelessness analyst and really excited to be here because this is a opportunity for us as staff to come and present a comprehensive update on the city's approach to homelessness. So tonight's presentation, we have a number of things that we're going to cover and we'll be providing a brief background and some context setting, as well as an overview of the city's approach and response to homelessness to date. For the council tonight, there are two recommended actions. The first is consideration of amendments to the city's camping ordinance. And then the second is consideration of contracts the city will need to enter into for the development and operation of the planned sanctioned camping area and for providing homelessness related services more generally in the city. So by way of background, as of the most recent point in time count In Marin County 2024, there are 1,090 individuals experiencing homelessness in the county. Of these individuals, 788 were unsheltered at the time of the count and 217 were chronically homeless. Now, I'll add that this represents a 2.77% decrease from the 2022 point in time count, but for San Rafael, the 2024 numbers are not yet available. So based off of the 2022 count, we estimate around 348 individuals experiencing homelessness in the city. But to supplement this work, the city did a survey last year of individuals who were living along the Mahone Creek path and of the people who were living there had done so for over a year and that two thirds of those people had lived in San Rafael for over a decade. Now, the county has had a lot of great success in recent years and housing individuals experiencing homelessness. Since 2017, they have been able to house 737 chronically homeless individuals and 94% of those folks remain housed to this day. Day, however, as we saw on the previous slide, I think particularly relevant for the discussion this evening is that there's still much more work to be done as we only have 291 shelter beds available in the county for over a thousand individuals. So turning our attention to San Rafael, we're going to spend some time on this slide. Not a year, but we'll be here for a little bit. The city has been effectively blocked from enforcing our camping on public property regulations since August of last year. So we've been at this now for over a year, really. And as you'll recall, it was this council who in 2023 had made amendments to the city's camping ordinance to comply with the then governing Martin v. Boise decision, and three days before that ordinance was to take effect act, the city was sued in federal court based off of the Americans with Disability act as well as claims that there was a state created danger. The court entered a temporary restraining order and then later a preliminary injunction that effectively blocked the city's ability to enforce these camping regulations from December to February of last year. And then this year, the city attempted in good faith to implement the direction of the court, which at the time it sought to have the city work with the California Homeless Union and individuals and members along the Mahone Creek Path area encampment to designate set campsites for individuals and establish voluntary compliance with the direction of the court. However, this work was ultimately abandoned because we were not able to achieve the level of cooperation that was needed in order for that approach to be effective. So shortly thereafter, the city refocused its attention towards amending the camping ordinance to address the concerns of the court and to create a regulatory framework that could we that we could ultimately use to mitigate the impacts of encampments. And the City council passed this updated ordinance in April of this year. Following this, the city filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit, and earlier this month the court granted this motion allowing the city to proceed with implementing the amended camping ordinance. And I'll have more to share on that implementation here shortly. However, I will note that during the time of the preliminary injunction, the city worked to identify other regulatory avenues to address the public health and safety concerns related to encampments in the city. As you may recall, in October and November of last year we enforced the fire code to abate fire risks associated with the proliferation of wooden structures and wooden pallets and encampments in the city. And then in December of last year, the city manager issued an order prohibited camping on Lindaro Street. And so, as you'll see on the slide here, we have a before picture of Lindaro street and then a picture of Lindaro street shortly after that order went into effect. And I'll add that for most of this summer, the city has been pursuing enforcement efforts aimed at addressing more illegally constructed structures within our city parks and public rights away. To date, the city has issued 49 notices resulting in 42 sites now complying with the city's regulations, and seven are currently undergoing an administrative appeals process where they actually have an administrative hearing scheduled for tomorrow. I will note as a statistic of this work that the city has removed over 31 tons of debris as a result of bringing these structures down. And it's important to note that when the city undertakes this work, we provide individuals with replacement tents and other items and also provide an option for individuals to store their public property for up to 90 days. So these next couple slides just show some before and after pictures of the city's work and addressing illegal structures and attempting to enforce on our camping ordinance. And so, as you can see, here are pictures in front of Marin Roofing along Francisco Boulevard West. Some additional pictures outside there. Here are some pictures along Anderson Drive, some before and afters, and then the Mahone Creek path as well. So, as Christine touched on in her opening remarks, there have been a number of legal, recent legal actions that have changed the landscape by which the city may regulate and address homelessness within the city. And so with that, I'd like to introduce Scott Emblem, who's one of our attorneys who help us with this, and he's going to speak to the Grants Pass ruling and its impacts on us here in San Rafael.

utterances.text: Scott thank you, John. Good evening, council members. So in the Grants Pass ruling, I think there's been sort of a public perception that, well, the Supreme Court ruled that cities can do whatever they want now, and so there shouldn't be any more home homeless people on the streets. Well, that's a gross overstatement of that ruling. The ruling addressed a narrow but substantial issue, but one issue, and that was the Eighth Amendment, whether it violates the Eighth Amendment of the United States Constitution to forbid people from camping or sleeping on streets unless a city provides sufficient space indoors for them to go to. The Supreme Court reversed the Ninth Circuit's decision that had established that Eighth Amendment doctrine. So it essentially removed one legal argument from the unhoused that are bringing lawsuits to try to establish their rights to be in certain places on public property. But that's just one argument. There are many arguments that have been raised in litigation, including litigation against the city of San Rafael. As the city manager mentioned, the injunction that has been tying the hands of the city of San Rafael for a year here was not based on the 8th amendment. It was based on other legal theories. And because this body amended its ordinance to try to comply with that injunction, we were able to get out of that injunction earlier, just a few weeks ago. But those other legal theories remain. And I, I guess the cautionary note is the concept that it is now free for cities to take whatever action a city wants regarding the unhoused population. From a legal perspective, apart from the practical concerns or the humane concerns from a legal perspective, there's still substantial legal risk to cities because these other arguments are out there. There are other arguments that I'm sure will be developed in other litigation. So unless the cities deal with the practical implications of the grants passed decision and the day to day homeless situations in those jurisdictions, they run the risk of substantial further litigation, which as you well know, is a drain on city resources, resources that can be better used to try to help the Idaho population. I can answer any questions when we're done with the presentation. Great, great.
